requiredKnowledge: Thermal harm from excessive infrared exposure
tasks.contextSummary: Infrared lamps used on vehicle paint.
solutionStructure: Name a thermal injury: skin, eye or tissue burns.

criteria.rule: Skin, eye or tissue burns, or damage to skin/surface cells caused by infrared heating.

acceptableAlternatives: The scheme accepts skin damage or surface-cell damage.
The scheme rejects skin cancer, cell mutation and sunburn.
dependencies: Do not substitute ultraviolet or ionising-radiation mechanisms.

commonErrors.description: Confusing infrared heating with mutation/cancer or ultraviolet sunburn.

syllabusMappings.rationale: The infrared hazard bullet explicitly identifies skin burns.

tasks.contextSummary: Compare infrared radiation and visible light from the lamps.
solutionStructure: Choose two distinct shared physical properties and state that each applies to both waves.

criteria.rule: One valid common property from the accepted pool.
A second distinct valid property; cap total at two.

acceptableAlternatives: Both are electromagnetic (or belong to the electromagnetic spectrum), transfer energy, are transverse, are non-ionising, can travel through a vacuum, or share the same speed in a vacuum.
The scheme also accepts reflection, refraction or diffraction as shared behaviors.
dependencies: Different wording for the same property receives credit once. Stating both EM and both part of the EM spectrum is one idea.
Same-speed comparison must specify a vacuum.

commonErrors.description: Using two synonymous statements rather than two distinct properties.
Claiming the waves always have the same speed in every material.

syllabusMappings.rationale: EM membership and common free-space speed.
Both waves transfer energy.
Shared reflection/refraction behavior.
Transverse nature of light waves.

requiredKnowledge: Relative frequency and wavelength in the electromagnetic spectrum
tasks.contextSummary: Compare properties of infrared and visible radiation.
solutionStructure: Infrared has a longer wavelength than visible light.
Infrared has a lower frequency than visible light.

criteria.rule: Infrared wavelength is longer than visible wavelength (or reverse comparison).
Infrared frequency is lower than visible frequency (or reverse comparison); retain the scheme's lower-energy concession.

acceptableAlternatives: Reverse comparisons for visible light are accepted.
The scheme condones saying infrared has lower energy; this is recorded as a source concession, not a claim that a lamp must transfer less total energy.
dependencies: Do not award a third mark for restating frequency as photon energy.
Comparisons must distinguish the two waves.

commonErrors.description: Describing different speeds in a vacuum.
Confusing the energy of an individual photon with total heater power.

syllabusMappings.rationale: Spectrum ordering by decreasing wavelength and increasing frequency.

tasks.contextSummary: Infrared travels 1.5 m at the supplied speed 3.0 × 10^8 m/s.
solutionStructure: Substitute: 3.0 × 10^8 = 1.5 / t.

criteria.rule: Correct substitution into speed=distance/time.
Rearrangement to isolate time.
Evaluation giving 5.0 × 10^-9 s.

acceptableAlternatives: 5 × 10^-9 seconds is accepted. Correct decimal equivalent is 0.000000005 seconds.
dependencies: Scheme specifies a one-mark deduction for a power-of-ten error; do not repeatedly penalise the same POT mistake.
The scheme's listed decimal 0.00000005 conflicts with its scientific answer. Preserve this discrepancy, never infer that both numerical values are physically correct.

commonErrors.description: Dividing speed by distance, or mishandling 10^8 in a denominator.
Power-of-ten error.

syllabusMappings.rationale: Distance/speed/time relation applies to this constant-speed wave transit.

tasks.contextSummary: White paint takes longer than black paint to harden under the heating lamps.
solutionStructure: Black paint absorbs infrared more strongly than white paint.
More energy reaches black paint in the same time, so it warms/hardens sooner under the stated conditions.

criteria.rule: Black is the better infrared absorber, or white the poorer absorber/better reflector.
Black receives more energy in equal time (or white receives less), or black warms faster.

acceptableAlternatives: Reverse explanations in terms of white paint are accepted.
The scheme explicitly awards both marks for saying black absorbs more energy/heat; two separately written sentences are not required.
dependencies: Credit physical ideas, not the number of sentences.
Do not confuse absorption of incident radiation with stronger emission from the surface.

commonErrors.description: Only stating that black hardens faster without explaining absorption.
Explaining the observation solely by black paint emitting more infrared.

syllabusMappings.rationale: Surface properties determine emission and absorption of thermal radiation.
Thermal energy transfer by radiation supplies the heating context.

tasks.contextSummary: From release below equilibrium until the first return to the initial equilibrium position.
solutionStructure: Acceleration magnitude falls to zero.
Spring extension and upward spring force decrease while weight stays constant.
The upward resultant therefore falls to zero at equilibrium.

criteria.rule: Acceleration decreases to zero; “decelerates” is not the requested statement.

acceptableAlternatives: Less stretched can express reduced extension.
Balanced forces is suitable if clearly limited to the equilibrium endpoint.
dependencies: The support alternatives have a two-mark group cap, not four available marks.
Do not equate falling acceleration magnitude with falling speed during this interval.

tasks.contextSummary: Two incident rays from air meet a water boundary on a scale diagram; explain, calculate and draw their paths.
solutionStructure: Draw a perpendicular normal at each point of incidence. Read angles to the normal, approximately 36° for A and 60° for B.
Use sin(r) = sin(i)/1.33 in degree mode: r_A ≈ 26.2° and r_B ≈ 40.6°.
Extend both rays into the water towards their normals, at the calculated angles, with arrows showing travel into water.
Water is optically denser than air; light travels more slowly in water, explaining the change in direction.
Total internal reflection cannot occur for this air-to-water direction. A critical-angle calculation does not answer this question.

criteria.rule: Award up to six distinct points from markingPointPool. Apply the joint MP1/MP2 cap if either ray bends in the wrong direction; MP3 and MP4 each earn at most one mark across both rays. Do not treat this aggregate cap as a single six-mark holistic criterion.

markingPointPool.rule: Ray A is refracted and changes direction; may be demonstrated by a ray drawn through the boundary.
Ray B is refracted and changes direction; may be demonstrated by a ray drawn through the boundary.
A correctly measured incidence angle for either ray: A 34°–38° or B 58°–62°.
Correct refraction-angle calculation for either ray; allow error carried forward from the incidence reading. Scheme expects A 24°–28° or B 39°–42°; may be shown on diagram.
Air and water have different optical densities. The historical note condones reversed density; preserve only in historical-source marking, not as correct teaching.
Light travels more slowly in water than in air; reverse comparison accepted.
No total internal reflection because light is entering optically denser water from air; ignore critical-angle values as irrelevant.

jointCaps.condition: Either refracted ray is drawn bending in the wrong direction.

acceptableAlternatives: Ray paths and angles can be evidenced on the diagram rather than repeated in prose.
MP4 allows error carried forward from the measured incidence angle; a measured-angle error does not automatically lose both angle marks.
Ignore reflected rays in this source scheme.
The scheme's reversed optical-density concession applies to historical MP5 only; no publisher correction has been obtained.
dependencies: Angles are measured relative to the normal, not the surface.
Apply the MP1/MP2 joint cap before the six-mark total cap.
Credit MP3 once and MP4 once even if both rays are measured and calculated.
A text-only adaptation cannot silently retain the original drawing demand.

commonErrors.description: Measuring the incidence angle from the boundary.
Drawing refraction away from the normal when light enters water.
Calculating a critical angle despite travel from lower to higher optical density.

syllabusMappings.rationale: Light can be refracted.
Draw ray diagrams for refraction.
Calculate refraction angles using refractive index.
Critical-angle reasoning must respect the direction of travel; no critical-angle calculation is needed here.
